opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I've thought about for many years, because it really sits at the heart of sim-to-real.

Early on, my instinct was that accuracy was everything. If the simulator doesn't match reality, whatever policy you train will exploit the gaps. Robots are very good at finding bugs in physics engines. You see a quadruped that learns to vibrate its foot in some weird way because the contact model gives it free energy. So a lot of our early work went into system identification: measuring motor dynamics carefully, modeling actuator latency, getting the contact parameters right. That paid off a lot. Some of the biggest jumps in our sim-to-real transfer came from modeling things like the motor's torque-speed curve or a few milliseconds of latency.

But over time I came to see it less as accuracy versus volume and more as two sides of one problem: you need a distribution of simulated worlds that covers reality. You can get there by making a single simulator very precise, or by making many slightly imprecise simulators varied enough that the real world falls somewhere inside. That's essentially what domain randomization does. You give up some accuracy in any one instance in exchange for diversity and scale, and the policy learns to be robust instead of exploiting one specific model.

In practice the best results come from combining them. You want the simulator accurate enough in the things that really matter for your task, usually contact, actuation, and latency for locomotion, and you don't need to be perfect on things the policy can be made robust to. Then you use massive parallel simulation, now thousands of environments on a GPU, to get the volume and diversity. If your simulator is fundamentally wrong in some systematic way, no amount of data will fix it; you just learn the wrong thing faster. And if it's very accurate but too slow to give you enough data, the policy won't learn the behaviors you want at all.

So my rough rule of thumb is: be accurate where errors are systematic and the robot can't compensate, and use scale and randomization where errors are random or the robot can adapt. As tasks move from locomotion to manipulation, with rich contact, deformable objects, and visual complexity, the accuracy problem gets much harder, and that's where I think combining simulation with real-world data and learned world models becomes really important. The balance keeps shifting, but the core question stays the same: does your training distribution cover the real world?

r001.rationale: The response says that many individually imprecise but varied simulations can cover reality, and that scale and randomization can trade off against per-simulation accuracy to produce robust policies.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this question gets at something people often misunderstand about sim-to-real in robotics. The intuition is that if the simulator were perfectly accurate, you'd just train in it and deploy, and the problem would be solved. But perfect accuracy is not achievable, and chasing it is actually the wrong objective.

The way I think about it is that simulation gives you two things that the real world can't: volume and diversity. A physical robot can collect maybe a few hours of useful data a day, and every failure costs you time, hardware, and sometimes safety. A simulator can give you millions of trials overnight across thousands of randomized environments. That volume is what lets a policy learn robust behaviors rather than memorizing one setup.

The tradeoff is that every increase in fidelity costs you speed. If you add detailed contact modeling, deformable objects, or high-resolution rendering, you might go from ten thousand frames per second to a hundred. So you're always trading data volume against how closely each sample matches reality.

My view is that you don't need the simulator to be right, you need it to cover reality. That's the whole idea behind domain randomization. If the real world's friction coefficient is somewhere inside the range you trained on, the policy has already seen it. The sim doesn't have to predict the exact value, it just has to make sure the truth isn't an outlier. In that framing, breadth of data is often more valuable than precision, as long as the simulator captures the right structure of the problem.

Where accuracy does matter is in the things the policy fundamentally depends on. For legged locomotion, that's mostly rigid-body dynamics, actuator behavior, and latency. If those are badly wrong, no amount of randomization saves you, because you're randomizing around the wrong center. So we spend effort on system identification for those core pieces, and we let everything else be cheap and noisy.

The other thing I'd add is that the right balance shifts over time. Early on, you want a fast, crude simulator to explore the space of behaviors. Once you know what works, you can afford to spend compute on higher fidelity to close the remaining gap. And increasingly, real-world data feeds back to calibrate or correct the simulator, so it's less a fixed tradeoff and more a loop you iterate on.

r001.rationale: The response says broad, high-volume randomized simulation data can make up for limited precision by covering real-world conditions, while noting that some core dynamics still need accuracy.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a tradeoff between how much experience you can generate and how useful that experience is for the real world. A very accurate simulator might be expensive to run, so you get less data. A simpler simulator can generate much more data, but the policy may learn to exploit things that don’t hold in reality. More data alone doesn’t solve that mismatch.

So the key question is: which aspects of the simulation need to be accurate for your task? For a walking robot, contact dynamics and actuator behavior can matter a lot. Other details might matter much less. You want to spend your computation on the parts that actually affect the behavior you’re trying to learn.

You can also vary the simulation parameters during training—things like friction, mass, or delays—so the policy learns to work across a range of conditions rather than depending on one precise model. But that range still needs to be reasonable.

Ultimately, I would judge the balance by how well the learned policy transfers to the real robot. The goal isn’t maximum simulation accuracy or maximum data volume by itself. It’s enough relevant accuracy, combined with enough diverse experience, to learn something that works in reality.

r001.rationale: The response says more data alone does not solve simulation mismatch and emphasizes accuracy in task-relevant aspects; it does not suggest that averaging over more data compensates for limited accuracy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the tradeoff depends on what you need the simulation to capture. For robot learning, you don’t necessarily need a simulator that reproduces every detail of the real world. You need it to capture the physical effects that matter for the task. If those are wrong, generating more data can just teach the policy to exploit the simulator’s mistakes.

At the same time, a very accurate simulator can be so expensive that you can’t generate enough experience to learn a robust policy. So I would aim for a simulator that is accurate enough in the important dimensions and fast enough to run at scale. Then you can vary things like friction, mass, and actuator behavior during training, so the policy doesn’t depend on one exact model.

Ultimately, the test is how well the policy works on the real robot. You use that feedback to decide where more simulation accuracy is worth the cost and where more diverse data is more valuable.

r001.rationale: The response says generating more data can reinforce a simulator’s mistakes and recommends balancing task-relevant accuracy with scale. It does not suggest that averaging over more simulation data compensates for limited accuracy in approximating real-world physics.
